Free habits tools

20 short exercises on habits, 2 to 7 minutes each, free and with no account needed. Open one and it runs right in the page.

The 20 tools

  • Design a morning you would actually do

    Build a realistic morning from pieces you would keep on a tired Tuesday, not an aspirational one you would abandon by the weekend.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • Habits: ease against impact

    Place the habits you are thinking about on a grid of how easy they would be to start against how much difference they would make.

    Grid · 5 min

  • A week of one tiny habit

    Pick one small habit and log each day whether you did it and how you felt afterwards. A week is enough to learn whether it is the right habit.

    7-day log · 2 min

  • The basics of a daily rhythm

    Tick the everyday rhythms that are currently in place: light, meals, movement, contact, sleep timing. Mood often follows rhythm more than we expect.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Which habit first

    Rank a list of common habit changes by which would most improve your life right now. Ranking forces a choice that a to-do list lets you avoid.

    Ranking · 4 min

  • One habit, taken apart

    Walk through a single habit you already have, good or otherwise: what comes right before it, what it gives you in the moment, and what it costs later.

    Guided writing · 7 min

  • How your habits tend to slip

    Rate how often a set of common ways habits fade has been true for you. Most people slip the same way every time, and knowing the way is half of catching it.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Where the friction is

    Set a dial for each stage of one habit, from remembering it to restarting after a miss. Most habits fail at one stage, not all of them, and the fix depends on which.

    Dials · 4 min

  • Keep, tweak, or let go

    Sort the habits you already have into ones to keep as they are, ones that need a small adjustment, and ones you are ready to let go of.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • Anchors already in your day

    Choose the things that already happen every day without effort. A new habit attached to one of them sticks far faster than one that floats.

    Card pick · 3 min

  • When the habit actually happens

    Mark the times across a typical week when one habit you are building actually gets done. The empty slots are not failures; they are the wrong slots.

    Week map · 3 min

  • The sentences that end a habit

    Turn over cards that show a sentence people say right before a habit stops, with a question on the back that keeps it going a little longer.

    Perspective cards · 5 min

  • Coming back after a miss

    A short guided restart for a habit that has slipped: name the gap, notice the story attached to it, shrink the habit, and do the two-minute version now.

    Guided exercise · 6 min

  • What runs on autopilot

    Divide 100 points across what fills the unplanned gaps in your day: the five minutes waiting, the hour after dinner. Gaps get filled by whatever is closest.

    Budget · 4 min

  • The bad-day version of your habits

    Build a set of habits shrunk to the size you could manage on your worst realistic day. A tiny version kept alive is easy to grow again; a habit dropped is not.

    Plan builder · 5 min

  • Signs a habit has taken hold

    Tick the signs that a habit you have been building has become automatic. Knowing where it is on the way to sticking tells you whether to hold steady or grow it.

    Noticing list · 3 min

  • Chosen or drifted into

    Sort the routines that make up your days by whether you chose them or drifted into them. Most habits arrive by drift, and drifted habits serve whoever built the surroundings.

    Sorter · 5 min

  • What you believe about changing

    Rate how often a set of beliefs about habits and change runs your thinking. Beliefs about size, speed, and perfection end more habits than any missed day does.

    Reflection · 5 min

  • Now versus later

    Place the habits you already have on a grid of how good they feel right now against how good they are for you later. The corners tell you what each one needs.

    Grid · 5 min

  • The person who does that

    Instead of planning a habit, describe the kind of person for whom it is simply normal, then find where you are already a little like them.

    Guided writing · 7 min

What these tools are, and are not

Every tool here is free and works without an account: choose cards, move dials, sort a list, follow a paced breath, or keep a seven-day log, and read back what you noticed at the end. They are built to make a vague feeling more specific, which is often the first useful step.

None of them diagnoses, screens for or treats anything, and nothing you see at the end is a score or a label. If something you notice worries you, a licensed therapist is the right next conversation, and the directory is free to browse.
